Shots are great, especially in the stand offs and one on one scenes. The framing has that classic old school western style where the characters are positioned carefully to build anticipation. Lighting and lens are very sharp. Sets and locations are great too. The dusty towns and wide open environments really help sell the western atmosphere. The sound design also feels old school. It lacks bass, I think. Everything sounds high pitched. Dialogues are obviously dubbed or rerecorded in the studio because some lines do not sync with the movements of their lips. The musical score sounds heroic, but emotionally I did not really feel it connecting with the story. Even by the end, I never fully felt the tension or triumph that the film was aiming for.
A tad slower of the three, some great shots, but seems to be more of a slog. Lee Van Cleef is a nice addition to the cast however. For the sake of the trilogy, it's ok, but not necessary.

"Alive or dead? It's your choice..." And it's also your choice whether or not to believe that this film it's good because it's of my opinion that this film is meh. However, it is leagues better than it's successor even though it gets a similar star rating. What I like about this film, like its successor, is the aesthetic of the film. The old wild west motif, the wild west set designs, and the wardrobe of that time are just a chef's kiss. However, what also needs to happen beyond that is there needs to be good/interesting and exciting characters as well as a good story that moves well. Unfortunately that isn't necessarily the case with this film like its successor. Although the Clint Eastwood and Lee Van Cleef characters are entertaining, sort of makes you appreciate them in following film more, the other characters in the film are boring and add virtually nothing to the overall story. They were all pretty boring besides the little boy at the hotel helping Eastwood's character as well as the old man living by the train tracks. Something I really find annoying in these films is the stupid hat shooting bit they do. It's obviously edited and fake thus making it super annoying and boring. Next segment already please! I also thought that this film was WAYYYYY TOO long and SLOOOW. There was no need for either of them regardless of the type of story they were trying to tell versus what they were actually telling. I didn't care that much for the film based on what I saw early on and so I didn't really pay attention for most of it. I honestly don't see the hype of these films one bit. They're not entertaining enough for me, they're too slow, too long, and not a whole lot in the character department in my opinion. All in all I also think that Sergio Leone is an overrated director just like Kubrick.

The train and its symbology is so strong in this film, and I can appreciate certain scenes, certain shots. I still can’t stand the dialogue of spaghetti westerns, and it is so enraging that it completely disengages me. Eastwood is handsome or whatever; ol Angel Eyes is back, he’s clearly apt for his role, I don’t mind him. They got an Italian guy to play the antagonist, a native Mexican, which works in absolutely no way, though I am a fan of the actor in his European films. The music is amazing! The movie even looks pretty cool. I just don't get it. I don’t feel anything from Westerns but infantilized by the writing. I don’t think the samurai:cowboy analogue works for me. Honor and respect are not the same.

Ok 90% of that movie makes way more sense when you realize that even though it’s the SAME ACTOR playing the villain as in a fistful of dollars, he is NOT Ramon, he is in fact Indio. I now feel silly for grunting slyly at the TV “aim for the heart, Ramon”. The excessive macho dick measuring contests for a little stale by the end. It felt like every scene was a standoff or sharpshooting some obscure object without flinching. It lost its gravitas. There were also way too many schemes to coherently follow. Even insignificant side characters had an agenda to throw the train of thought off the tracks. It was a knot of plot twists that you couldn’t untangle. Also, why’d the bitch shoot herself when she could’ve just as easily shot el Indio. Seemed unwarranted and could’ve given el Indio a more powerful backstory if there was a more relatable backstory, or at least fed into the psycho side more. He’s literally crying over some girl he raped after sliming her man. Showing any emotion at all feels contradictory to his character, but perhaps this adds to the chaotic nature of his character. Also, I know this was the 60s, but the Rojos and El Indio is just mental. Red and Indian? Like Indians are the cliche villain in Westerns, but to call Mexicans Indians in their own language seems like a unnecessary shot fired. Regardless of the over saturation of the macho, the colonel was a sweet addition. Threatening the macho of our Manco was refreshing. The cinematography felt like it took more of an advantage of the landscape, and the opening and closing shots were some of my favorites (for of a person shot off a horse in the opening, colonel riding off into the sun at end). The opening credits also had an intriguing graphic that flowed along the landscape. Fun. Color on set, lighting, and costuming felt a little more bland than fistful, but the night effects were better with the blue light as opposed to just darkening the screen in fistful. The audio syncing was yet again pretty criminal, but I won’t give too much grief given the era.

Bon pas grand chose après le visionnage du premier film. Les deux films se ressemblent beaucoup dans la production, toujours le même dynamisme à la caméra, des effets spéciaux et maquillages similaires. Par contre gros changement au niveau de l’écriture du film (cette fois pas de plagiat lol), avec alternance de moments dynamiques et d’autres moments plus creux mais c’est globalement bien rythmé on voit pas le temps passé. Le jeu d’acteur est toujours super, sauf sur les chutes (surtout quand ils meurent mon Dieu quelle horreur)…. La musique est grandiose, on commence à entendre les similitudes avec le dernier film de la trilogie.
